In this sense, this book is part of a larger project which seeks to explore the ways in which anthropologically inspired approaches can stimulate social and political theory. It is to be situated in the encounter between anthropology and sociological thinking, transporting an anthropological concept into the heart of the social sciences writ large. Such an interdisciplinary dialogue, which draws on anthropological insights in the theorization of the modern, has to be carried out with extreme caution. As we have argued elsewhere in more detail (Thomassen 2013a), it is indeed risky to apply concepts beyond the field of investigation in which they emerge. Ever since the inception of the social sciences, anthropology has constantly been used by social theorists as a starting point for the construction of alterity, a platform from which to think ‘the Other’ of modernity (Faubian 2000). Such a use of the ‘primitive’ does of course go back to some very central traditions in European philosophy and thinking – back to the Enlightenment, and back to seventeenth century contract theory – and its need of the exotic Other as a negative or positive reference point. Anthropology has often served to sustain various incompatible views of the ‘human’ or of ‘human nature’, to fantasize about an ‘original state’ of human affairs or ‘state of nature’ (Kuper 1988). Far from belonging only to Hobbes or Rousseau, Romanticism or speculative philosophy, this construction of alterity has been perpetuated within the allegedly most empirical and objective traditions in social theory, including functionalism and Marxism. The notion of an original primitive society was quite a central foundation for arguments made by Marx and Engels, which relied much on the then existing anthropological speculation on ‘origins’ that dominated early evolutionism. Anthropological works on primitive peoples stimulated Marx and Engels’ idea of ‘primitive communism’, a view of an undifferentiated group of people living freely together without centralized power or private property. Durkheim operated a much similar conceptual divide between mechanical and organic solidarity, instrumentally using dubious data on ‘archaic’ people to explain modernity. Even Freud saw anthropology (and the Australians once again) as a shortcut to establishing the universal rules of the deeper psyche (Kuper 1988: 105–22). These tendencies were later smuggled in through the back door by the leading social theorists across the Atlantic, most visibly in branches of social theory inspired by Durkheimian and/or Marxian approaches. In America, Parsons aimed to construct an evolutionary scheme of social development and social organization. Parsons basically posited primitive society as ‘undifferentiated’, at the social, cultural and personality levels (Faubian 2000: 252); and in this way ‘it’ still served as a starting point of difference, from where to articulate the unfolding modalities of differentiation that according to Parsons had guided social development (Parsons 1960). The primitive also takes centre stage in Habermas’ evolutionary narrative of communicative action. In Theory of Communicative Action [TCA] (1984, 1987), Habermas makes the overall argument that in modernity ritual has declined and been replaced by rational discourse. Habermas can make

Chapter 5 Liminality in the Transition to Modernity: The Case of Thomas Hobbes and René Descartes The search for the ground, thus, remains recognizable as the reality experienced even in the modes of deformation. However much the symbolisms of deformation may express existence in untruth, they are equivalent to the symbolisms of myth, philosophy, and revelation. (Eric Voegelin, The Ecumenic Age) In the past, it was the work of the intellectuals to sublimate the possession of sacred values into a belief in ‘salvation’. The conception of the idea of salvation, as such, is very old, if one understands by it a liberation from distress, hunger, drought, sickness, and ultimately from suffering and death. Yet salvation attained a specific significance only where it expressed a systematic and rationalized ‘image of the world’ and represented a stand in the face of the world. For the meaning as well as the intended and actual psychological quality of salvation has depended upon such a world image and such a stand. (Max Weber, The Social Psychology of the World Religions) This chapter will approach the larger time period that followed what Huizinga termed the ‘waning of the Middle Ages’ in Europe from around the end of the fifteenth century to the mid-seventeenth century that is often referred to as ‘early modernity’. Early modernity, following here Huizinga and Voegelin, was not experienced as a ‘breakthrough’ or a passage toward a more ‘mature’ modernity, but rather as a total collapse of order, an age of anxiety, an ‘age of great confusion’ (Voegelin). In the terminology proposed here, it was a liminal age. The age was in desperate search for new ordering principles within politics, philosophy and science. Within this larger field of emergence, two very specific but also famous cases will be invoked: the live experiences and related thought systems of the contemporaries, Thomas Hobbes and René Descartes. In the confronting of liminality – the loss of taken-for-granted structures – the disorder of the early modern age was overcome with the ideational and political-institutional structure that was established with the ‘moment of Westphalia’, and with Cartesian science laying the foundations for modern thought. We argue that this new order was in a critical sense liminal at its core, jointly establishing fear and doubt (archetypical liminal experiences) as foundational.

Liminality and the Modern114 Hobbes and Descartes: Why and How to Read them Together Thomas Hobbes and René Descartes are rarely read together. There are obvious reasons why not. Thomas Hobbes developed a radically negative view of the human person on the basis of which a new political order was proposed. René Descartes developed a new and radical version of truth and science built upon the safe ground of the rational human self. Hobbes was one of a handful of prominent thinkers carefully selected to comment upon Descartes’ Meditations. Here Hobbes openly went up against some of Descartes’ most fundamental ideas, including the argument of the cogito itself. Descartes replied, and in no less harsh tones, that ‘as long as my critic refuses to come to terms with me about the meaning of words, none of his objections can be other than frivolous’ (Descartes 1997: 209). Taken at face value, Hobbes and Descartes talked past each other. It seems reasonable to conclude that Hobbes did not have a very high opinion of Descartes, and vice versa (Sommerville 1992: 20). It is also a commonplace to assert that the two thinkers were in fact occupied with two very different and incommensurable projects. Descartes’ main focus was not politics, and he proposed no theory of the state to compete with the Hobbesian construct. Hobbes, on the contrary, was highly involved in science, and was, just like Descartes, engaged in developing a general philosophy. However, we read Hobbes today almost exclusively because of his political ideas. Even if contemporaries considered Hobbes a scientist (Malcolm 2002: 51) his interest in geometry and optics is included in the literature on Hobbes mostly to the extent that it is regarded as having shaped his view of politics (for an exception, see Pacchi 1965). We treat the two thinkers as forefathers within two different realms: Hobbes is the founder of modern politics, while Descartes is the founder of modern science and philosophy. Put simply therefore, Hobbes and Descartes are rarely read together because they posited almost opposite philosophical anthropologies as the building stones of their thought, and because their works took off (or rather, were carried off) in different directions. The important connections between Hobbes and Descartes were taken up most explicitly by Richard Tuck (2002 [1988] and 1998). Tuck discussed how the two thinkers were drawn into the same academic landscape via the group of philosophers gathering around Mersenne, and indicated the extent to which Hobbes may have developed his philosophy through his reading of Descartes. Tuck also stressed how their projects resembled each other: they both wanted to establish a new philosophy, and they agreed that whereas human perception of the world was irremediably faulty, a new departure must be made by regarding sense-impressions as the object (rather than the basis) of investigation. Indeed, beyond their disagreements (which were indeed substantial), Hobbes and Descartes may very consciously have considered each other rivals in laying claim to this idea (Tuck 2002: 28–31). The idea was revolutionary because while accepting the scepticism of antiquity, it offered an alternative: a modern philosophy and a new scientific world image departing from the self. Hobbes and Descartes were not ‘too different’, but all too similar.

Liminality in the Transition to Modernity 115 The argument we wish to propose here does not build on the actual correspondence between Hobbes and Descartes as this was mediated by their mutual friend, Marin Mersenne; nor will the connections between the two thinkers be biographically or textually traced. Rather than focusing on their substantial disputes or disagreements, it will instead be suggested that Hobbes’ and Descartes’ epistemological claims represent complementary ways of instituting modernity. The parallels between Hobbes and Descartes exist at the level of morphology, in the kind of ‘absolute’ boundary they draw around the modern state and the modern self, respectively. Their writings can be compared although the order that they establish is substantially different, and although they principally apply it to two very different kinds of ‘interior’: the sovereign state and the sovereign self. These underlying parallels, and the joint Weltbild they served to conjure, were captured by Borkenau in his landmark work, Der Übergang vom feudalen zum bürgerlichen Weltbild: Studien zur Geschichte der Philosophie der Manufakturperiode (Borkenau 1976 [1936]). Secularity in Modernity One of the landmarks of the modern world-view that developed from the seventeenth century was the introduction of secular principles in both thought and political organization, and Hobbes and Descartes are rightly seen as founders in exactly this sense: in the grounding of their systems of thought they abandoned, once and for all, a divinely-ordained legitimization. In seeking out a new ground, they both discovered a new type of principle which could supersede and replace religion and its dangerous divisive tendencies that had shattered Europe during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. In most readings, Hobbes and Descartes are therefore also primary figures in the rationalization of thought and practice that paved the way for a wider secularization process, as a new boundary between the secular and the sacred would slowly become accepted and institutionalized. In this sense, the development of thought in the mid seventeenth century is rightly considered a forerunner to the Enlightenment, and both Hobbes and Descartes must beyond doubt be considered as path-breaking transitional figures toward European modernity. The debate between secular and religious interpretations of Hobbes has been raging since at least 1953, when Hood published The Divine Politics of Thomas Hobbes as a challenge to the more dominant secular interpretations, which tend to see Hobbes’ religious writings as opportunistic and in no way foundational for his real aim: creating a secular political theory built onto a philosophical materialism. However, the debate has been an integral part of the reception of both Descartes’ and Hobbes’ works ever since they were published in the seventeenth century. The exact terms of the debate have changed, but the main questions remain: is religion central to their systems of thought? If so, then how so? Are their religious writings really combinable with their science? Did Hobbes and Descartes really care about God and the Bible, or were they (consciously?) paving the way for the final victory of a secular, scientific world-view?

It will be argued that a breakthrough of ‘absolutism’ within both political theory and rational philosophy took place around the middle of the seventeenth century,1 as exemplified in the work of Hobbes and Descartes, who, beneath their apparent differences and disagreements, shared to a substantial degree a common problem, to which they offered structurally similar solutions. These similarities can be spelled out by linking thought to experience, and to experience of a certain kind: human reactions to liminality. This chapter thus seeks to exemplify the general thesis that certain elaborations of liminal periods may prove decisive for the way in which a new order is established, at both the personal and societal levels, and that modernity on that account can in a crucial way be understood as a permanentizing of liminal conditions. Following Borkenau, it was those answers and their routinization form the critical underpinning of a modern world-view. The concept of liminality has its relevance to political and social theory precisely here, as it was developed by anthropologists to make sense of human experience and processes of subjectivation during moments of dissolution, in other words, during social and political crises; and such a perspective is equally applicable to the history of thought. The concept of liminality helps to bring into perspective the otherwise strange and very radical turn to self-foundation, evident in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. A founding characteristic of liminality is indeed to replace the outside chaos with an order of the inside, having radicalized and brought to exhaustion doubt and scepticism through personal and collective reflexivity. In the classical ritual passages to manhood one of the most common exercises is to force the initiands to cut off the sensory apparatus from the ‘world’ in order to gain an inward vision (often received in a dream-like state), a vision of truth that the initiand must elaborate and make manifest in the shaping of his new personality. As described by van Gennep (1960) and Victor Turner (1969), during ritual passages, the initiands or the neophytes are brought to question most radically their own sensory apparatus, just as they challenge social order by setting themselves apart from any normally accepted social rules from their betwixt and between position; they become nameless, timeless and socially unstructured, existing in a floating state of being, even as they acquire throughout the liminal period the necessary knowledge and experience in order that their transformed beings may eventually re-enter society and take up their new roles. It is by no means a coincidence that the driving principles in Hobbes’ and Descartes’ systems of thought relate back to two fundamental human experiences in liminality: fear (of violent death) and doubt (how can I know anything? What is my role in the production of truth?). The perspective adopted here is not entirely new; rather, the anthropological approach proposed speaks in evident ways to existing frameworks of analysis in political theory. The eschatological and ultimately millenarian structure of Hobbes’ political thought was, among others, emphasized in the analysis offered by J. G. A. Pocock. As argued by Pocock, Hobbes’ most radical innovation was to employ (and not delete) sacred history as a new instrument of secular power (Pocock 1989: 179; see also Martinich 1992). Methodologically, Pocock sought to establish a new type of history of political thought in which the available language and what could be termed the ‘taken-for-granted’ universe of the political thinker function as the basis of the textual interpretation. Pocock used as a theoretical basis the notion of paradigms, taking his cue from Thomas Kuhn’s The Structure of Scientific Revolutions. Pocock argued that political discourse has to be analysed by considering the paradigms within which a thinker poses problems and offers solutions (following here Kuhn, who said that the larger framework of scientific questioning was only very rarely put into question, and that ‘normal science’ was mostly a practice of puzzle-solving). By implication, Pocock argued that we have to analyse Hobbes by taking seriously the ‘intellectual paradigms’ within which

(Descartes, Discourse on Method) The general break with the mediaeval world has often been described as an ‘anthropological revolution’, placing man as the origin of meaning. This revolution occurred over several centuries affecting all the sub-domains of human thought and activity, and reformulating most basically the role of man in the production of truth, order and beauty. Breaking the ‘cosmological shell’ of the mediaeval universe implied a new emphasis on human creativity and human agency, and opened up new horizons of another man-made world. In philosophy this anthropological revolution can be identified as reaching its apex with Descartes and the Cartesian cogito, which on the standard view is seen as the beginning of modern philosophy, if not indeed of modern thought (Sorell 1997: xxix). If so, modern philosophy and thought originate with a very specific self-discovery that needs to be analysed in its own terms. One strong desire cuts across Descartes’ authorship: the need to undo a philosophy based on knowledge inherited from the past. We should not rely on ‘what others have thought’, as stated the third rule in Rules for the direction of the mind (Descartes 1997: 8). Descartes was here taking issue with the ancients, in particular with the scholastic tradition, but in general Descartes attacked customs and habits of the mind that people employed without use of proof-testing. He wanted to establish a method that could eliminate human errors from the chain of logical reasoning. In Discourse on Method (published in 1637), Descartes presented his scientific method, which was further developed in Meditations on First Philosophy, first published in Latin in 1641. Descartes’ philosophical trajectory can itself be analysed as a ritual passage. This is as implicitly argued in the short, suggestive Introduction to Descartes’ work by Chávez-Arvizo who likens Descartes’ metaphysical project to a ‘voyage’ of truth discovery undertaken by the nameless and timeless meditator (1997: xv). As stressed by van Gennep (1960) each step of the ritual passage (separation, liminality proper and re-integration) is subdivided into several rituals that test and ultimately transform the initiand who goes through the trial. The first stage of separation most often happens physically as the initiands are physically removed from their society, literally losing all hitherto existing reference points and prior knowledge. The tripartite structure is most clearly present in Meditations on First Philosophy. In the First Meditation Descartes starts his mental voyage by separating himself from all pre-established ‘opinions’; the method of doubt progressively takes apart all preconceived knowledge, starting by fundamentally doubting sense-based beliefs, doubting whether it is even possible to know whether one is asleep or awake, arriving at the utmost point of radical

In the Second Meditation Descartes overcomes the void and finds ‘something which is certain’, the cogito: the fact that I am thinking, therefore I exist. This new-gained certainty is immediately tested against further doubts. Descartes’ procedure here closely resembles the importance in ritual passages of proving one’s new identity through testing. The following meditations aim at testing the existence of God (the Third Meditation) and of material things (the Fifth Meditation). He faces the entire gamut of un-truths that thrive within his world, and drives out the evil. The ritual passage is an individual voyage, but with universal implications: Descartes is simply laying bare a truth which is inbuilt in the universe, and kindly offers truth to the world. In fact, Descartes is both the initiand and the master of ceremony in the ritual passage. He establishes universal reason discovered in his individual self. When taken as a singular eruption of thought this sounds terribly like the idea of a madman, but the exercise had historical predecessors and a larger social field of emergence. Descartes and the Demon of Error Descartes’ bearing on the Christian atmosphere of seventeenth century Europe are very clear, and have been pointed out in the biographical literature. One major indirect impact was the general ‘internalization of religion’, produced by the Reformation and the Counter-Reformation (Gaukroger 1995: 25). The rival churches converged in the attempt to transform the church from public to private, to make faith a matter of personal internalized conviction. One of the tools was the generalized use of the ascetic technique of self-retreat, combined with the negative definition of the self as it had developed in the monasteries and as formulated in the idea of contemptus mundi that preached the hatred of the body and the world, the pervasiveness of sin and the fleetingness of time (Gaukroger 1995: 25). Descartes applied in converted form some of the ascetic techniques and contemptus mundi to himself and to his philosophy: he engaged in his own kind of therapeutic self-reform similar to the monastic experience; he hated the fluctuating truths of his perceptions, the weaknesses of his body, the un-truths which guided the world, the pervasiveness of error; and he had a sharp sense of the fleetingness of conceptual thought. Descartes’ own relationship with the church was full of tensions. Although he remained a confessional Catholic, he dismissed most of scholasticism, and attacked the Aristotelian philosophical premises that were then ruling Catholicism. This brought him into trouble with the Catholic Church, and therefore partly with his

Descartes would constantly have to assure his Jesuit brothers that his rationalization of the world was not in contradiction with the teachings of the Church. Yet, as a resident in the Netherlands (from 1628–1649), Descartes’ ideas inevitably provoked those with Orthodox Calvinist ideas, and Descartes was not wise enough to stay out of trouble in his host country, where he eventually became looked upon with suspicion as well (Watson 2007: 221–43). Descartes’ language is on this point most direct in Meditations on First Philosophy, and especially in the Fourth Meditation, Of the true and the false, where he tackles the problem of ‘error’. Descartes talks about the will that ‘easily falls into error and sin, and chooses the evil for the good, or the false for the true’ (1997: 166), putting thus truth and good, and error and evil on the same plane. True enough, in his own introduction to his Meditations (ibid.: 123–33), Descartes is keen to stress (before his Catholic audience) that the ‘sin’ he will talk about relates only to errors in deciding between the true and false, and not to questions of faith (ibid.: 132); yet his drawing on the same vocabulary is at the same stroke further underlined; and Descartes, as we know, will not refrain from proving the existence of God. This drove Descartes to the question: why did God put error into the world? The question is identical to another question, which God’s children normally address from an early age: why did God put evil into the world? If God decides everything, why is there evil? The believer is puzzled and arrives at the conclusion that either evil was some kind of secret force that slipped out of God’s control (Satan as the jealous angel), or that God (since He is, after all, almighty) let evil loose to punish mankind. Descartes found no satisfaction in either answer. Indeed, he found such answers part of the error he wanted to undo. He proved that error had not been God’s intention at all. Error had come about by an erroneous path taken towards cognitive truth, and in his Fourth Meditation Descartes claims to have set us back on the right track of true reason (ibid.: 166–9). Having singled out error as the demon, Descartes wanted to establish some ground on which error was defeated by truth. That ground was his self. From there, Descartes went on to redesign himself out of a solitary vision. His road to liberation went through a refuge into self, and from this refuge he could reach salvation from error. Knowledge saves. Although one should not take such statements at face value, Descartes himself claimed that from an early age he received signs concerning some kind of revelation of truth, that he would dedicate his life to the pursuit of truth, and that his possible success in this self-imposed task would serve as a new basis of universal order and knowledge (see Rodis-Lewis 1992).

Liminality in the Transition to Modernity 123 Descartes and the New Ground of Order A few further points about Descartes and his new philosophy must be made explicit at this point. Descartes can surely be considered a Weberian ‘switchman’: he is one of those thinkers who managed to change the shape of the subject before him. Weber invoked the metaphor of switchmen in the context of his comparative study of the world religions (1948), invoking the prophet as ideal type. Weber never worked out a full-blown typology for intellectual figures, but in so many ways a thinker like Descartes performs as a prophet: he diagnoses the illnesses of his age, establishes a new truth through inward reflexivity, and then offers the truth to the world as a revelatory key to a new epoch. He posits himself as the medium through which the entire world can bring about a change. The radical nature of Descartes’ philosophy is visible by the way in which he ‘clears the ground’ by totally erasing the relevance of pre-existing knowledge and experience. In The Passions of the Soul Descartes characteristically declared that he feels obliged to write ‘as though I were treating of a matter which no one had ever touched on before me’ (1997: 358). Descartes’ attack on almost all existing knowledge is repeated elsewhere. In The Principles of Philosophy, first published in 1644, Descartes dismantled what he here called the ‘prejudices of childhood’ (1997: 305), the source of all errors: our reliance on sense-impressions. And also here Descartes proceeded to replace the world of errors with a new-found certainty, the cogito. The gnostic thinker creates a void so that he can erect a new edifice from scratch and bestow order on the world – the whole world. How can one understand Descartes’ ‘ordering experience’? The exact road taken by Descartes towards pure reason is not our issue here. It went through doubt, and it went through absolute divisions of body and mind, faith and reason. In Discourse on Method, Descartes had argued that the self was ‘completely distinct from the body’ and could exist without it (Descartes 1999: 25). Paving the way for the cogito, this was the much known and criticized mind-body dualism that Descartes installed. Indeed, Descartes was openly taking departure from the Aristotelian account of soul which denied the mental any reification as separate substance. The Hobbesian problem of order was therefore not some distant abstract, philosophical preoccupation, neither was the general shattering of truth that worried Descartes. Both Hobbes and Descartes developed their thoughts during the Thirty Years’ War. The continued existence of war and unrest was their ‘normal’ background experience. Rites of Passage: Liminality and the Role of Transition In terms of general interpretation, there are strong indications that the ritual jumping in all of the cases combines the two fundamental and universal types of rites of passage originally described by Arnold van Gennep: rites that mark the passage of an individual or social group from one status to another and those which mark transitions in the passage of time (which, as in the gol ritual, is often connected to harvest) (van Gennep 1960: 10). The rites are quite simply classical examples of ritual passages in liminal time and space. The liminal character is underlined by the polluted status of the jumper during the period that runs up until the jumping event, surrounded by various (evidently culture-specific) taboos. In their liminal phase, the jumpers represent a challenge to stability and order, and must not be brought into contact with the normal world. For the individual jumper, the rite is a way to demonstrate manhood. Various culture specific versions of jumping rites have without much doubt represented a ritual passage into manhood – or a continued demonstration of that manhood status. In many cases it may therefore have involved a real, substantial transformation of a man’s identity and social status. This personal aspect, however, is in all cases tied to a wider social cosmology and mythology that renders the jumping meaningful. The jumping ritual is therefore also a collective ritual whereby a society moves from one moment into another, signifying a passage or marking of time in a wider cosmological calendar. The material from the Pacific region points to a feature that may be shared across cultures: namely that the tree pole itself (here a tower) represents an axis of transition and transformation. Although this again is almost impossible to ‘prove’, it would tie the jumping rituals to central features of shamanistic belief systems and to the symbolic role of trees as representing both life and death and transformation in a wide variety of cultures. Indeed, the word ‘axis’ may even be etymologically connected to ‘tree’. The PIE word for oak was *dreu, which metonymically would come to signify tree in Northern European languages, with *aiks becoming the proto-Germanic word for oak. Linguists claim *aiks to be of unknown origin and with no certain cognates outside Germanic languages, but the closeness to axis (deriving from PIE *aks) seems striking. The Latin word for tree, arbor/arbos is no less interesting. It derives from alba, which means ‘white’ and ‘light’, and also denotes that moment of ‘white light’ in the morning between night and daylight: dawn, daybreak, or as indeed in modern Italian, alba.

Liminoid phenomena have liminal qualities, but at the same time they do not really belong to rituals and are therefore also not stages or phases in a ritual. Liminality and the Modern186 Turner suggested a perhaps oversimplified dichotomy between symbolic systems of a ‘traditional’ and a ‘modern’ type, arguing that ‘we must distinguish between symbolic systems and genres which developed before and after the Industrial Revolution’ (1982: 30). The liminoid is the modern break from normality, a playful as-if experience. Here Turner explicitly invoked forms of entertainment such as theatre and sports, art and even literature as the modern equivalents of ‘culture in the subjunctive’. As rituals have faded away or lost much of their function and meaning, they have become replaced by the performative genres (ibid.). The as-if culture that develops in these genres, like ritual itself, involves a kind of reflexive playfulness that may generate novelty and innovation in self-understanding and perhaps even in shaking up or sometimes reversing social roles, hierarchies, values or established views, and with possible ramifications for the wider public sphere. However, Turner stresses that such modes of expression no longer belong to a rather fixed scheme of social ritual, shared by the entire social group. Post-industrial society is much too fractured for such ‘unified’ ritual experiences; specialization and rationalization have splintered the social fabric alongside a general process of individualization. Meaning has become personal. Expressive culture develops into several specialized fields and genres, and nobody is any longer forced to undergo the same ritual passages. Rather, individuals themselves seek such liminoid experiences on a voluntary basis. Liminoid phenomena develop within relatively independent genres, and the engagement with these phenomena becomes tied to the individual consumption of the ‘out-of-the-ordinary’ as a commodity. Instead of the collective and obligatory we have the individual and the optional. This decoupling of the liminoid from a ritual sequence also means that liminoid genres, in a larger sense, are no longer ‘context-sensitive’. The liminoid has no reference to the rhythms and cycles of nature and human life, as was the case in premodern ritual. The out-of-the-ordinary is decoupled from calendrical, biological and social structural cycles. The timing and placing of the liminal become random or idiosyncratic. In short, the liminoid develops outside that framework of ritual passage which was so fundamental to the very concept of liminality as proposed by van Gennep. Cultural performance in the ritual-liminal mode therefore stands in opposition to the industrial-liminoid forms of entertainment and performance. Liminality has survived, but it has changed; and thus, Turner, argued, we need a different term to capture this ‘as-if-liminality’: what he termed the liminoid. Turner’s view belongs to a general framework of understanding modernization as individualization, specialization, rationalization and also secularization; the liminoid survives, but no longer as collectively agreed upon rituals at the core of society, but rather as individualized searches for excitement at the (spatial and temporal) fringes of the social. And yet, Turner clearly saw in these genres the seeds of renewal and the positive survival of the playful.

From Liminal to Liminoid to Limivoid 187 From Liminoid to Limivoid The importance of these insights could hardly be exaggerated. Turner’s framework has had a massive effect on the study of liminal experiences, and has become a household term in anthropology and cultural studies, particularly for scholars working within the fields of arts, leisure and tourism. It may be that Turner argued both too much and too little at the same time. On the one hand, and as argued also by Rowe (2008), Turner’s distinction between the ‘ritualistic’ and the ‘non-ritualistic’ is overdrawn, and perhaps not necessary at all. Football games, to state the obvious, are highly ritualized performances, for both practitioners and the spectators involved. They are even tied to a calendar (the season, initiated by pre-season games) that to quite a few people has huge symbolic importance, as supporting and following one’s team through the season comes to serve as a real identity marker. Turner may also be overstating the individualistic nature of liminoid experiences. For the specific case of bungee jumping (and perhaps more markedly so for other extreme sports) community bonds do in fact develop alongside these practices. While certainly open to individual choices, they are clearly still social phenomena. This is so, first and foremost, for practitioners of the sport, who even develop their own language and codes of behaviour. It also becomes clear from the fact that many bungee posts are placed at the centre of leisure parks or erected in the context of festivals. Being seen, being recognized and sometimes accepted into a group are essential aspects of contemporary jumping activities. Put simply, the actual experience is therefore not completely individualized, to the extent that jumpers will almost always be accompanied by friends or family who witness the jump (and/or who participate in it as well). It must also be noted how jumpers frequently share their accomplishment with a potentially global readership via Tweets, blogs or YouTube films. Of course, it must at the same time be stressed how the social reference group ‘participating’ in the event is individually selected and/or created; and the entire undertaking does of course remain voluntary. Sports and extreme sports may on this score be very different from the performance of other genres of activity, like the writing of poetry and painting, genres that are indeed tied to an essentially solitary experience, but which Turner lumps into the same category. In other words, it is often the case that the performance of extreme sports takes on highly ritualistic forms, although clearly no longer within a religious framework. Contemporary bungee jumping may even, in some cases, replicate some even more evident aspects of a ‘classical’ rite de passage. Daring activities, such as bungee jumping, are sometimes arranged on stag nights or bachelor parties. This is the time when a man who is about to get married celebrates the future event by spending an action packed day with friends – and sometimes bungee jumping for the groom- to-be is a central part of the programme. The celebration on the stag night marks and initiates the coming of his status-transformation: from unmarried, to married.

This also means that the in-between experience itself has undergone a radical transformation: the ‘other side’ of the experience is no longer a transformed or re-generated human being; neither is it an entry into another season or period of a cosmological calendar. The other side of the experience is quite simply ‘death’, a death which is of course not real, but which is ‘nearly’ felt, just for the fun of it. Chapter 8 Liminal Politics: Towards an Anthropology of Political Revolutions 1 This chapter further explores the applicability of the concept of liminality, now with reference to transition as understood in the context of a specific set of sociological phenomena: political revolutions. The motivation behind this argument is so obvious that it probably needs no justification. We are evidently living through yet another epoch marked by the revolutionary appeal. Revolutions evidently represent clear-cut instances within political history of liminal figurations: drastic moments in which previously existing structures crumble and collapse, where norms and hierarchies are turned upside down. But what does it imply to study political processes from an anthropological perspective, and what exactly does it imply to adapt the concept of liminality to the study of political revolutions? This is the question we would like to discuss here. Is there an Anthropology of Political Revolutions? In 1961, Peter Worsley opened his paper assessing the anthropology of rebellions and revolutions with the following statement: ‘A survey of the social anthropological literature on rebellions and revolutions is a simple undertaking, for it is the absence of such analysis that is so striking’ (1961: 26). Half a century later, having witnessed several waves of revolutions across the world, as well as radical, abrupt, and irreversible changes in social norms, political systems, and cultural values, surely anthropology has by now an established tradition of studying political revolutions. Or has it? There is certainly an anthropological tradition of studying protest and resistance. The Manchester school in political anthropology developed a focus on conflict and political rebellion, but that did not involve a proper study of political revolutions in modern state societies. As we saw above, in 1963, on his way toward America, Victor Turner had his decisive reading experience of Arnold van Gennep’s Rites of Passage, and developed a processual approach to the study of change via liminality (1967; 1969). This approach, however, has rarely been systematically or directly applied to political transformation, despite Turner’s own hints in that direction. If the word ‘revolution’ figures in anthropological readers it most often refers to social change within a long-term process, as in the ‘industrial’ or ‘Neolithic’ revolutions. Alternatively, it refers to paradigmatic changes within anthropological theory itself, as in ‘linguistic revolution’. Since the 1960s anthropologists have frequently depicted epistemic changes in thought as revolutions. But they apparently have much less to say about those that take place around us and continue to shape the world in which we live. Half a century after Worsley’s call for a social anthropological engagement with political revolutions, research on the subject is thoroughly dominated by political scientists, political sociologists and historians. Of course, these disciplines are bigger and arguably more powerful than anthropology, and that they dominate a research area so evidently central to their subject matter is by no means strange. In fact, sociology started with Saint-Simon and Comte, and one of their central claims was that, with the revolution, France had arrived at a crucial moment of transition. Their work focused on the historical process leading to this juncture, and on the solution that would end the crisis (Szakolczai 2009: 144). The question of the revolution marked academic and political debates in nineteenth century France and beyond, and was intimately related to both nation-state formation and the emergence of the social scientific disciplines: what were the real consequences of the revolution? In what way could the revolution be seen as a completely new starting point? The question was central to Saint Simon, but in a crucial way it underpinned sociology all the way into the twentieth century, as the discipline took shape. And for a discipline focused on social change in modernity this should hardly come as a surprise. But why are anthropologists so strikingly silent about political revolutions? Political scientists write volumes about them without consulting the anthropological literature. Foran’s edited book Theorizing Revolution (1997), despite engaging at length with the cultural dimensions of revolutions (especially via Selbin’s important contributions), makes almost no reference to any work of anthropology, and John Dunn’s much-quoted study of political revolutions (1989) does not mention anthropology either. The list could be continued, but these writers can hardly be blamed, for the neglect comes from within anthropology itself. This neglect is even more surprising given that anthropologists in a very general way tend to side with the ‘people’ over and above institutional power structures. Political revolutions involve, as a minimum, some degree of mobilization of those ‘ordinary people’ that are normally the focus of our ethnographic accounts. Moreover, anthropologists have been very sympathetic toward social and political emancipation, especially in colonial and postcolonial situations. It could even be argued that anthropology has an unarticulated affinity with political revolutions, if perhaps a slightly problematic one. From the 1960s onward, a good portion of anthropologists certainly shared, at the theoretical as well as ideological level, Marxist-inspired appeals to revolution as a way of overcoming social inequality and colonial repression. This was evident, for example, in the French neo-Marxist schools of anthropology built around Godelier and Meillassoux.

Throughout the twentieth century, once it became evident that the Western working classes had turned into docile bodies, the search for revolutionary potential was directed toward Russian workers, then Chinese peasants, then Third World movements, then peasants in general, then women, then students, then some of these categories in combination. We start by examining what Turner himself said most directly about political revolutions in his late work, and especially in his famous essay The Anthropology of Performance which also became the title of his last book (published posthumously). The state is the administrator of legitimate violence, said Weber. It is also here that an anthropological reading of the struggle over symbols and meanings becomes relevant or even necessary. Chapter 9 By Way of Conclusion: Out of Liminality The ritual sequence, or rather, the processual, playful order that Arnold van Gennep detected and named in his study of cultural ceremonies, contains at the centre, in the middle of everything, a phase and space of liminality. This was not something that van Gennep invented or a theory he ‘constructed’. It was something he literally dis-covered; it was already there, and Marcel Mauss could have done better than to ridicule van Gennep’s ground-breaking work for ‘stating the obvious’. If there is one reason that we still read Mauss’ work on gift-giving today, then it is not only for its honest and engaged use of the existing ethnographic record for a comparative purpose: it is precisely this ‘A-ha!’ sensation that it brings to the reader in an almost timeless way. It says something so simple and evident that we simply have to give in and realize that giving, receiving and giving back lies at the heart of meaningful sociability. Everywhere. Arnold van Gennep’s dis-covery of the tripartite structure of rituals became the ordering device of his immense life’s work. It was an illumination for himself. After his death, and with the English publication of Rites of Passage, it also became his belated claim to fame. Most people who know the name Arnold van Gennep know him for that one idea. Contrary to what one might have expected, this did not lead to any thorough revisiting of the life and work of Arnold van Gennep. Sociologists still today do not consider him. Arnold van Gennep is the thinker of liminality. His own life was much stamped by critical threshold experiences, and also by his failed rite of passage into institutionalized academia.
